title: Federal Records Officers
subject: Constitutional Law
stem: A federal judge is already handling a subpoena fight over student-aid audit files from a chain of vocational schools. For similar federal enforcement suits, Congress creates temporary federal records-officer posts. Each officer may schedule production, manage routine discovery disputes, and submit recommendations to the assigned Article III judge. The judge reviews the officer's work, and the officer's assignment ends with the case. Congress authorizes the federal district courts to select the officers.

choices.A: The appointment route is invalid because every federal officer must be appointed by the President with Senate confirmation.
choices.B: The appointment route is valid only if Congress itself confirms each records officer.
choices.C: The appointment route may be valid if the records officers are inferior officers and the appointing body is a court of law.
choices.D: The appointment route is invalid because courts may never appoint officers assigned to matters connected to executive enforcement.

rightExplanation: C is correct. The Appointments Clause requires principal officers to be appointed by the President with Senate confirmation. But Congress may vest appointment of inferior officers in the President alone, in heads of departments, or in courts of law. The officers here have limited case-specific duties, work under Article III judicial review, and serve only for the assignment. Those facts support inferior-officer treatment. If they are inferior officers, district-court appointment may be valid.

wrongExplanations.A: This choice attracts students who remember the default method for principal officers. The breaker is that the Constitution gives Congress alternative appointment routes for inferior officers.
wrongExplanations.B: Congress may create the office and choose a permissible appointment route for inferior officers. The breaker is that Congress does not itself appoint or confirm them outside the constitutional methods.
wrongExplanations.D: The executive-enforcement setting makes this answer tempting. The breaker is that courts of law may appoint inferior officers when the office is compatible with judicial functions and constitutional limits.
